data.title: U.S. court approves New Jersey PFAS settlements totaling $2.5B
data.description:
A federal judge on Friday approved more than $2.5B of ‌settlements reached by the state of New Jersey with DuPont (DD), 3M (MMM), Chemours (CC), and Corteva (CTVA) to resolve claims over pollution attributed to PFAS, or "forever chemicals."

The judge said the settlements reached last year were fair, reasonable, and adequate, and served ​the public interest, calling the total value an "impressive windfall" given the risks ⁠of litigation.

The settlement with DuPont (DD) entities, valued at more than $2B, is on its own the largest environmental settlement ever achieved by a single state, and the combined settlements resolving the claims against the DuPont entities and 3M (MMM) are valued at ~$2.5B; Chemours (CC) ‌and ⁠Corteva (CTVA) were part of DuPont prior to spinoffs.

The companies face other litigation over PFAS contamination, including a lawsuit last month by New ​York Attorney General Letitia James.

data.title: Data center operator Switch confidentially files for IPO - report
data.description:
Data center operator Switch confidentially filed for a US initial public offering. 

A Switch listing could come as soon as November, according to a  Bloomberg report on Friday, which cited people familiar with the matter. Bank of America (BAC), Citigroup (C),  Goldman Sachs (GS), JPMorgan Chase (JPM), and Morgan Stanley (MS) are working on the offer.

Switch, which is majority-owned by DigitalBridge (DBRG), has been working on a funding round led by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and could seek a valuation approaching $50 billion, including debt, Bloomberg reported last month.

Separately, Ben Horowitz, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz,  is joining Switch’s board, according to the latest Bloomberg report.

Representatives for Switch, Bank of America, and JPMorgan declined to comment to Bloomberg. Spokespeople for a16z, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

data.title: HEI outlines $170M base rate increase plan while seeking 1,650 GWh renewables in Hawaii procurement
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Hawaiian Electric Industries (HE) Q2 2026

Management View

  • CEO Scott W. Seu framed Q2 around regulatory execution and affordability, highlighting that the PUC “granted our request to recover approximately $350 million of WMP spending through the Exceptional Project Recovery Mechanism” and that HEI now “plan[s] to request recovery of WMP costs through securitization rather than the EPRM,” with EPRM used only for costs that “may not be eligible for securitization.”
  • Seu said the company is operating in “a transitional year as we prepare for our expected reset of rates in 2027,” and detailed a $170 million proposed base rate increase phased over 2 years, with $125 million proposed to start in 2027 and an interim decision requested by December 18, 2026 so new rates can begin January 1, 2027.
  • Seu described competitive procurement scale as a key strategic lever: “It will be one of the largest competitive procurements for generation resources in state history, seeking nearly 1,650 gigawatt hours of variable renewable energy, 465 megawatts of grid forming resources and 111 megawatts of firm generating capacity,” and added HEI is also requesting an all-fuels RFP by end of 2026.
  • CFO Paul Ito reported GAAP results were affected by a Maui wildfire settlement accounting change: “For the second quarter of 2026, we generated net income of $123.2 million or $0.71 per share,” including “a noncash accounting adjustment” that reduced the remaining settlement liability “from $1.44 billion to $1.3 billion,” with the benefit expected to “reverse over time through the accretion of interest expense over the next 3 years.”

Outlook

  • Management reiterated the operational backdrop as a transition year ahead of 2027 rebasing, with Ito noting, “we do expect higher O&M for the full year as we progress through a year of transition ahead of our rate rebasing,” and tied mitigation to “rate rebasing,” potential PBR “Phase 6” changes, and “internal efficiency measures,” including exploring “in-source more work versus outsourcing to contractors.”
  • On wildfire mitigation cost recovery, Ito said, “we plan to finance our $350 million in approved wildfire mitigation plan CapEx through securitization,” and “later this year, we’ll be submitting our request to the commission for the financing order.”
  • The analysts estimates dataset provided in the prompt did not meet the required fiscal-quarter formatting (Q1–Q4), so no estimates comparisons are included.

Financial Results

  • Ito said excluding Maui wildfire settlement-related impacts and Pacific Current asset-sale losses, “consolidated core net income and EPS were $22.5 million and $0.13,” and “utility core net income for the quarter was $32.6 million,” citing higher interest expense from “last September’s debt issuance” and higher O&M driven by vegetation management, maintenance, overhead, and underground inspection.
  • Liquidity was described as ample: “As of the end of the second quarter, on a consolidated basis, total liquidity was approximately $1.3 billion,” including $52 million holding-company unrestricted cash and $186 million utility unrestricted cash, plus roughly $550 million each of additional available liquidity at the holding company and utility.
  • On credit, Ito said, “in July, S&P upgraded HEI and Hawaiian Electric 1 notch to BB-,” and noted the upgrade reflected WMP progress and PUC support; he added this followed “Moody’s 1 notch upgrade” in April.

Q&A

  • Michael Lonegan, Barclays: Asked whether securitized WMP spend should be removed from rate base/capital plan through 2028 and how to think about rate-base growth; Executive VP & CFO Ito answered, “to the extent that we do get approval to securitize the wildfire mitigation plan expenses, then that would not be part of rate base that would be recovered through the securitization,” while noting the commission must still rule on eligibility.
  • Lonegan, Barclays: Asked when the next rate case could be filed given the rebasing structure; Senior VP Joe Viola replied, “we’re going to rebase rates right now for the next 5-year multiyear rate plan,” and “we would expect we’d be rebasing rates through some process in roughly the 2032 time frame.”
  • Lonegan, Barclays: Pressed for detail on O&M running above inflation; Ito split O&M into episodic storm costs, deliberate spend-ahead items (vegetation management and maintenance), and structural increases (insurance), and said mitigation includes rebasing, Phase 6 alignment, and efficiency actions; CEO Seu added HEI is “taking a pretty holistic viewpoint.”
  • Lonegan, Barclays: Asked about JERA’s proposal to establish a regulated generation utility; CEO Seu said the filing has not “formally kicked off any part of the process,” emphasized decisions should be “in the best interest of all customers,” and stated HEI “will participate fully” in any PUC process.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analyst tone was neutral to slightly skeptical, concentrating on rate-base implications of securitization, timing of future rate proceedings, the magnitude and drivers of above-inflation O&M, and uncertainty around a potential new regulated GenCo.
  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks (credit actions, PUC approvals) and more explanatory in Q&A, with repeated emphasis on process and approvals still required, including Ito’s “to the extent” framing on securitization eligibility.
  • Versus Q1, management focus shifted from settlement milestone execution and fuel-price working-capital mechanics to securitization strategy, procurement scale, and how structural O&M pressures will be addressed through rebasing and PBR changes.

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Q2 added a specific pivot to securitization under Act 258 for WMP recovery, replacing earlier reliance on EPRM recovery mechanics discussed as recently approved by the PUC.
  • Q2 introduced new procurement detail and scale (1,650 GWh renewables; additional firm generation options up to 500 MW on Oahu pending a PUC “demonstration of need”), whereas Q1 messaging centered more on settlement payment execution and the Waiau approval framework.
  • Analyst focus narrowed in Q2 to securitization’s rate-base impact, rebasing cadence (pushing expectations out to ~2032), structural O&M pressures, and the potential market structure implications of JERA.

Risks and Concerns

  • Ito said HEI “continue[s] to expect to realize the maximum penalty under our fuel cost risk-sharing mechanism,” and also “do[es] not expect to achieve the same level of PIM and shared saving mechanism rewards as we did last year,” adding, “We are currently expecting to accrue a loss from PIMs and SSMs for the full year 2026.”
  • On regulatory risk, Seu said the PUC required proof of need before advancing “such a significant procurement” for up to 500 MW of additional firm generation on Oahu, and management said it will respond with analysis and stakeholder engagement.
  • Ito flagged sustained cost pressure from “higher interest expense” and structural insurance increases, while stating HEI is reprioritizing work and pursuing regulatory modifications to better align recovery with cost trends.

Final Takeaway

Management characterized Q2 as a regulatory- and execution-driven transition quarter, emphasizing PUC-backed wildfire mitigation recovery progress and a planned shift to securitization for $350 million of WMP CapEx, a $170 million rate-rebasing request with an interim decision sought by December 18, 2026, and a major competitive procurement agenda targeting 1,650 GWh of renewables and new capacity resources; CFO commentary centered on core earnings pressure from higher interest and O&M, while highlighting liquidity of about $1.3 billion and improved credit trajectory following rating upgrades tied to wildfire risk mitigation progress.

data.title: MSC Income Fund outlines $40M combined share purchases and targets leverage ramp over next 3-4 quarters
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: MSC Income Fund (MSIF) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "Before we provide our normal quarterly updates, I want to start by congratulating Nick Meserve on the recent announcement of his planned transition to Chief Executive Officer of the Fund in the fourth quarter of this year." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Dwayne Hyzak)
  • "We are pleased with the Fund's performance in the second quarter, which resulted in an annualized return on equity of 15.9% and a significant net fair value appreciation in the Fund's investment portfolio." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "The Fund generated adjusted net investment income, or ANII, of $0.33 per share on the quarter, or $0.36 per share on a before-taxes basis." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "The Fund finished the quarter with an NAV per share of $16.51, a 4.0% increase from prior quarter." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "We're pleased that the Fund exited its investments in one high-performing lower middle market portfolio company, Centre Technologies, in the second quarter at a realized gain of over $11 million and a meaningful premium to its March 31 fair value." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "The Fund's Board of Directors declared regular monthly dividends for the fourth quarter of $0.11 per share... And a supplemental dividend of $0.03 per share, payable in September, resulting in total dividends payable in the fourth quarter of $0.36 per share." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "Going forward, the Fund expects to maintain a dividend policy... generally consistent with the Fund's ANII before taxes per share." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "We're pleased to announce that the Fund's Board of Directors recently authorized a new open market share repurchase plan under which the Fund may repurchase up to $20 million of Fund shares beginning in September 2026 and ending in February 2027" (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "Main Street also authorized a new share purchase plan to purchase up to $20 million of the Fund's shares... resulting in a total of $40 million of potential purchases between the Fund and Main Street" (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "Main Street... voluntarily agreed to permanently waive approximately $260,000 of incentive fees earned for the second quarter... resulting in total incentive fee waivers of $1.4 million over the last year." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "The Fund's total investment income for the second quarter was $35.7 million... an increase of $1.6 million, or 4.7%, from the first quarter." (CFO & Treasurer Cory Gilbert)

Outlook

  • "As of today, I would characterize the private loan investment pipeline as average." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "We remain confident in our ability to generate attractive new private loan investment opportunities and grow the Fund's investment portfolio over the next several quarters." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "It's really hard to predict how long it'll take us to ramp. If you were to kind of use a best guess, I'd say the next 3 or 4 quarters." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • "We expect M&A activity will be higher in the second half of the year, and expect that activity to continue to grow our pipeline." (Managing Director Nicholas Meserve)
  • Compared with Q1’s pipeline framing, management again said the pipeline was "average." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak; Managing Director Meserve)

Financial Results

  • "The Fund's total investment income for the second quarter was $35.7 million... consistent with Q2 2025 and an increase of $1.6 million, or 4.7%, from the first quarter." (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)
  • "The second quarter included income considered less consistent or non-recurring in nature of $2.2 million." (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)
  • "The Fund's adjusted NII before taxes in the second quarter was $16.3 million, or $0.36 per share." (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)
  • "During the quarter, the Fund recorded a net increase in the fair value of its investments of $19 million, representing the impact of $9.9 million of net realized gains and $9.1 million of net unrealized appreciation." (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)
  • "Overall, the Fund's operating results for the second quarter resulted in a net increase in net assets of $29.3 million, or $0.65 per share." (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)
  • "As of quarter end, the Fund had investments on non-accrual status comprising 1.9% of the total investment portfolio at fair value and 5.8% at cost." (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)
  • "As of quarter end, the Fund's regulatory asset coverage ratio was 2.13 and its net debt to NAV ratio was 0.85." (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)
  • "Our $150 million of October 2026 notes mature on October 30, and we are actively evaluating our options for addressing that maturity ahead of the October date." (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)

Q&A

  • Kenneth Lee, RBC Capital Markets: asked about leverage ramp timing; CEO Hyzak said, "If you were to kind of use a best guess, I'd say the next 3 or 4 quarters," while highlighting repayments as "another governor" on ramp pace.
  • Kenneth Lee, RBC Capital Markets: asked about attractive segments and terms; Managing Director Meserve said, "not focused in any one industry" and on pricing, "we're probably around the same spot we've been for the last quarter or so. Spreads have come wider since January."
  • Arren Cyganovich, Truist Securities: asked about competition with an "average" pipeline; Managing Director Meserve tied it to muted sponsor activity, saying, "if we see that volume pick up, I think the overall competition level and potentially spreads and terms go a little wider."
  • Arren Cyganovich, Truist Securities: asked about non-accrual levels; CEO Hyzak said non-accruals are "a little elevated" and framed a longer-term level as "something that's 2% on a cost basis," while Meserve noted some names remain on non-accrual during multi-year recovery, "we'll recover that over multiple years."
  • Heli Sheth, Raymond James: asked about balancing deployment vs. repurchases; CEO Hyzak said, "we're trying to take a balanced approach" and called buybacks "a productive way to create value for the shareholder" while also saying "we also want to continue to deploy capital."
  • Heli Sheth, Raymond James: asked about software opportunities; CEO Hyzak said, "software has never been a focus area for us" and "I still don't think that's an area that we would expect to be active in."
  • Melissa Wedel, UBS: questioned sizing and timing of the $20 million repurchase plan; CEO Hyzak said, "we don't have a super scientific analysis," and tied sizing to combined capacity, "we really look at the sizing of the plan at $40 million."
  • Melissa Wedel, UBS: asked what drove NAV increase beyond Centre; CEO Hyzak said Centre’s premium was "[$1.5 million] higher than the fair value at 3/31" and added, "it's not the sole driver," citing other marks and equity co-investments in private loans.
  • Melissa Wedel, UBS: asked whether equity appreciation implies deal activity; CEO Hyzak emphasized fundamentals first, "EBITDA is growing... they're using free cash flow to de-lever," with exits later influenced by inbound interest and "the valuation multiple increase."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts were slightly negative to pressing on capital allocation and credit quality, focusing on competition, non-accruals, and buyback sizing (e.g., "Non-accruals ticked up" and "how do you come to the size of that particular authorization"). (Arren Cyganovich, Truist Securities; Melissa Wedel, UBS)
  • Management tone was slightly positive and confident in portfolio quality and tools to create value, pairing buyback support with deployment intentions (e.g., "we remain confident" and "balanced approach"), while using qualifying language on timing (e.g., "hard to predict"). (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak; Managing Director Meserve)
  • Versus Q1, management introduced more concrete shareholder-value actions (new repurchase plan) and leadership transition specifics, while keeping a similar stance on an "average" pipeline and macro uncertainty language. (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Leadership change was newly announced in Q2: "Nick Meserve... planned transition to Chief Executive Officer of the Fund in the fourth quarter of this year," with Hyzak moving to "Executive Chairman." (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • Capital return tools shifted from expired plans in Q1 ("each of which expired at the end of March") to a newly authorized windowed plan in Q2 ("beginning in September 2026 and ending in February 2027") plus matching Main Street purchases. (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • Portfolio marks swung from Q1 fair value decline ("net decrease... of $2.9 million") to Q2 appreciation ("net increase... of $19 million"), alongside a larger quarter’s net asset increase. (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)
  • Credit metrics moved higher on non-accruals from Q1 ("1.1%... at fair value and 4.2% at cost") to Q2 ("1.9%... at fair value and 5.8% at cost"). (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)

Risks and Concerns

  • "Given the current economic uncertainty that exists across certain parts of the economy, we are diligently working to stay in front of the Fund's portfolio companies to understand their exposures to changing environments." (Managing Director Meserve)
  • Management highlighted repayment pace and muted M&A as constraints on leverage and portfolio growth, with Hyzak citing "accelerated repayments" as a potential drag on ramping leverage. (CEO & Chairman of the Board Hyzak)
  • Refinancing risk was flagged around near-term maturities: "$150 million of October 2026 notes mature on October 30" and management is "actively evaluating" solutions. (CFO & Treasurer Gilbert)

Final Takeaway

Management highlighted Q2’s stronger portfolio marks and NAV increase alongside a shareholder-return package centered on a new $20 million MSIF repurchase authorization (matched by a $20 million Main Street purchase plan) and a dividend policy management said is expected to remain generally consistent with ANII before taxes per share. Executives framed the private loan pipeline as “average,” expected leverage to ramp over the “next 3 or 4 quarters,” and pointed to continued monitoring of portfolio-company exposures amid economic uncertainty, while acknowledging that non-accruals were “a little elevated” versus longer-term targets and that the October 2026 notes maturity is an active capital-structure priority.

data.title: AIG targets general insurance expense ratio below 30% in 2027 while contracting Lexington property
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: American International Group (AIG) Q2 2026

Management View

  • CEO Eric Andersen said AIG delivered “strong second quarter results” and stated the company “remain[s] on track to achieve” the financial commitments from its 2025 Investor Day, highlighting adjusted after-tax income per diluted share of $2, adjusted after-tax income of $1.1B, and core operating ROE of 11.1%.
  • CEO Andersen framed the pricing backdrop as “transitioning from an extended phase of broad positive pricing into a more selective environment,” citing increased capacity across E&S carriers, MGAs/MGUs, delegated authority, and ILS structures, with particular pressure in property.
  • CEO Andersen said that given “ongoing rate pressure,” AIG has “intentionally continued to contract our Lexington property portfolio in targeted areas,” adding that this drove “a meaningful 9 percentage point reduction in premium retention in Lexington property” and reduced overall North America growth “by over 3 percentage points.”
  • CEO Andersen highlighted strategic expansion, stating, “during the second quarter, we announced an agreement to acquire Everest Insurance operations in Colombia,” describing Colombia as “one of the largest and fastest developing insurance markets in Latin America.”
  • CFO Keith Walsh said, “Second quarter General Insurance adjusted pretax income was $1.5 billion,” and reported net premiums earned of $6.2B, underwriting income of $686M, and total catastrophe charges of $210M, including “$75 million in net losses related to the Middle East conflict.”
  • CFO Walsh addressed reserve actions and confidence, noting U.S. excess casualty strengthening of $74M and adding, “We continue to feel confident with our reserve position.”

Outlook

  • Management did not provide explicit EPS or revenue guidance in the prepared remarks or Q&A; the discussion centered on cycle management, underwriting discipline, and Investor Day targets.
  • CEO Andersen said AIG will not “chase growth blindly,” and emphasized, “profitability is always the North Star,” while still stating, “we do see opportunities for growth.”
  • CFO Walsh reiterated the cost target, stating, “we are on track to bring our expense ratio below 30% for full year 2027,” and pointed to a trailing 12-month expense ratio of 30.7% as of June 30, 2026.

Financial Results

  • CEO Andersen reported underwriting income of $686M and said the accident year combined ratio as adjusted was 88.1%, while net premiums written increased 9% (11% excluding North American Property), supported by Global Commercial and Global Personal growth and “recent strategic transactions.”
  • CFO Walsh said General Insurance adjusted pretax income was $1.5B and described the earnings drivers as “higher underwriting income and higher interest income, partially offset by lower income from our alternatives portfolio.”
  • CFO Walsh detailed prior-year development as $145M favorable, citing favorable loss experience “most notably in U.S. workers’ compensation of $177 million and U.S. property and special risks of $79 million,” partially offset by “strengthening in U.S. excess casualty of $74 million.”
  • CFO Walsh reported investment results and mix, including total net investment income on an APTI basis of $908M, and said alternative investment income was $13M versus $48M a year ago, adding that private equity “posted a loss of $8 million.”
  • CFO Walsh said AIG returned $904M to shareholders in Q2 (including $641M of repurchases and $263M of dividends) and added, “In May, we sold approximately 25 million shares of Corebridge common stock for $710 million, which was the remainder of our holdings.”

Q&A

  • Taylor Scott, Barclays: Asked about premium leverage, “excess capital,” and managing through a softer market; CEO Andersen replied AIG prefers “growing into the capital base” but remains focused on “returning capital through buybacks and dividends,” and said reaching ROE goals requires “strong execution around underwriting, around expense discipline, investment income, capital management.”
  • Meyer Shields, KBW: Asked whether social inflation is moderating; CEO Andersen responded, “we haven’t seen anything that says that it’s moderating at this point, and we’re certainly not building that into our pricing.”
  • Meyer Shields, KBW: Asked about IBNR in accident years prior to 2023 given excess casualty actions; CFO Walsh said AIG remains “in our expected range of outcomes” and added, “We’re not seeing material or any deterioration,” describing the 2023 move as “simply prudent.”
  • Brian Meredith, UBS: Asked about acquisition ratio mix-shift effects on loss ratios; CFO Walsh said mix is driving a “loss ratio tick up a bit,” but added, “Our accident year combined ratio adjusted margins have largely held.”
  • Brian Meredith, UBS: Asked whether pricing conditions push AIG toward inorganic growth; CEO Andersen said AIG will continue to look for “strategic opportunities where we can deploy capital and get the right return.”
  • Michael Zaremski, BMO: Asked how premium growth supports ROE goals; CEO Andersen cited cycle management and said strategic transactions helped prepare for a tougher growth year, while Jon Hancock said, “we’ve been expecting it… we’ve been preparing for it, and we’re managing it for sure,” flagging energy pricing as an area where “we’re not happy with what we see going on in the market.”
  • Michael Zaremski, BMO: Asked if AIG Assist is visibly improving throughput; CEO Andersen said, “We’re seeing more business. We’re quoting more business,” and described emerging “broker level insight” as “early days.”
  • Rowland Mayor, RBC: Asked to size the Convex quota share premium contribution; CEO Andersen said AIG has “not really broken out the pieces,” adding that the “reinsurance tailwind in the first quarter… largely dissipated in the second.”
  • Rowland Mayor, RBC: Asked about AI-related corporate debt exposure; CFO Walsh responded, “We don’t have significant allocations to AI-specific related debt.”
  • Pablo Singzon, JPMorgan: Asked what is driving Global Personal improvement; CEO Andersen cited “underwriting actions… reinsurance savings, lower acquisition costs,” and emphasized continued investment behind Accident & Health momentum.
  • Elyse Greenspan, Wells Fargo: Asked about the premium growth guide and second-half caution on property; CEO Andersen said, “it’s still a little early in the year,” and reiterated discipline over chasing growth.
  • Elyse Greenspan, Wells Fargo: Asked about leverage targets; CFO Walsh said AIG is at 17.6% debt to adjusted capital and added, “we run with a conservative leverage in the company.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analyst sentiment was slightly negative to neutral, with repeated probing on cycle softness, premium leverage/ROE mechanics, reserve prudence, and sustainability of growth; questions on social inflation and growth guidance carried the most skepticism.
  • Management sentiment was slightly positive in prepared remarks and more defensive-pragmatic in Q&A, emphasizing discipline and confidence; CEO Andersen said, “we’re not going to chase growth blindly,” while CFO Walsh repeatedly steered the framing toward trailing metrics and process confidence.
  • Versus last quarter, tone shifted from transition-focused (leadership change) to execution-focused under CEO Andersen, with more emphasis on selective growth, property contraction actions, and reserve/process explanations.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Leadership and messaging changed as Eric Andersen moved from President (Q1) to CEO (Q2), and he closed Q2 by thanking former CEO Peter Zaffino, saying, “His partnership throughout this transition has really been fantastic.”
  • Net premiums written growth slowed from 18% in Q1 to 9% in Q2, with Q1 benefiting from a January 1 reinsurance tailwind that management said “largely dissipated” by Q2.
  • Underwriting profitability remained strong but moderated sequentially, with the accident year combined ratio as adjusted moving from 86.6% (Q1) to 88.1% (Q2), alongside increased focus on property price pressure and deliberate Lexington contraction.
  • Analyst focus broadened from Q1’s AI-heavy discussion and E&S property concerns to Q2 emphasis on ROE/premium leverage, reserve prudence in excess casualty, and the sustainability of growth in a more selective pricing environment.

Risks and Concerns

  • CEO Andersen highlighted “competitive pricing pressure” in property from expanding market capacity and said Lexington property retention declined due to targeted contraction; management framed this as deliberate underwriting discipline.
  • CEO Andersen said AIG is watching energy and aviation where pricing “does not fully reflect heightened exposure,” while CFO Walsh quantified Q2 catastrophe losses including Middle East conflict losses.
  • On casualty severity risk, CEO Andersen said social inflation has not shown signs of moderating and is not being assumed in pricing.

Final Takeaway

Management presented Q2 as continued execution on Investor Day commitments, led by strong underwriting results, disciplined capital return, and selective growth. The call emphasized active cycle management—particularly contracting Lexington property amid rate pressure—while continuing to invest in AI-enabled underwriting and claims productivity, pursuing targeted transactions (including the announced Colombia acquisition agreement), and reiterating the goal to reduce the General Insurance expense ratio below 30% for full-year 2027.

data.title: Starz raises 2026 adjusted OIBDA growth outlook to mid-single digits while targeting ~2.7x leverage after $100M credit facility increase
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Starz Entertainment Corp. (STRZ) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "We delivered another strong quarter and entered the back half of 2026 with significant momentum across the business." (President, CEO & Director Jeffrey Hirsch)

  • "Season 5 has grown its audience from the first season 5 years ago, a rare achievement in today's television landscape." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch) "Fightland premiered as STARZ's second best-rated new IP launch of all time." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

  • "The content portfolio in the quarter generated the second-highest audience engagement quarter of all time." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch) "This marks the fourth consecutive quarter of engagement growth since we separated." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

  • "We are now raising our adjusted OIBDA growth forecast and our unlevered free cash flow guidance." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch) "We also continue to see a clear and accelerating path toward our leverage target and our 20% margin target." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

  • "We launched a new partnership with Peacock during the quarter, making STARZ available as an add-on subscription to the platform for the first time." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch) "This partnership allows us to market STARZ to an additional 48 million subscribers." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

  • "Total revenue in the second quarter was $308 million." (Chief Financial Officer Scott MacDonald) "OTT revenue was $221 million." (CFO MacDonald) "Linear and other revenue was $87 million." (CFO MacDonald)

  • "Adjusted OIBDA was $60 million for the quarter, ahead of our expectations." (CFO MacDonald) "Unlevered free cash flow was negative $15 million in the second quarter and positive $66 million year-to-date." (CFO MacDonald)

Outlook

  • "We expect this revenue trend to continue, putting us on a solid path toward achieving our outlook of positive annual OTT revenue growth in 2026." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

  • "We are raising our 2026 adjusted OIBDA growth guidance from low-single digits to mid-single digits, and we remain confident in achieving our 20% adjusted OIBDA margin target in the back half of 2027." (CFO MacDonald)

  • "We are raising our unlevered free cash flow outlook to the mid- to upper-end of our previously provided $80 million to $120 million range." (CFO MacDonald)

  • Analyst-estimate comparisons were not included because the provided estimates data uses an invalid fiscal-quarter format relative to the required Q1–Q4 convention.

Financial Results

  • "OTT revenue was $221 million, growing year-over-year for the first time since the fourth quarter of 2024." (CFO MacDonald) "ARPU continued to improve in Q2 as the April price increase flowed through the base." (CFO MacDonald)

  • "Cash content spend was $182 million for the quarter." (CFO MacDonald) "Now that we have exited the Universal Pay-2 agreement, we expect to report full-year cash content spend below $600 million on our cash flow statement." (CFO MacDonald)

  • "Net debt was $566 million as of June 30, 2026, and our adjusted OIBDA leverage ratio was 2.9x." (CFO MacDonald) "Today, I am pleased to announce that we have obtained firm commitments to increase our credit facilities by $100 million." (CFO MacDonald)

  • "We recorded the associated restructuring charge of $147 million this quarter." (CFO MacDonald) "We continue to expect this to be the final content restructuring charge of this magnitude going forward." (CFO MacDonald)

Q&A

  • Vikram Kesavabhotla, Baird: asked about Fightland acquisition and engagement patterns; President, CEO & Director Hirsch: "it's the second best premiere of new IP in the history of STARZ" and "Fightland is about $2.5 million per episode cheaper" while President of Domestic Networks Alison Hoffman added "really seeing an influx of win-backs or lapsed-users coming back to the platform." (President Hoffman)

  • Vikram Kesavabhotla, Baird: asked about licensing Power to Netflix; President Hoffman: "we are the exclusive home of the Power Universe" and said the move to Netflix for mature "Power" is "a way for us to introduce the franchise to new audiences." (President Hoffman)

  • Brent Penter, Raymond James: asked about monetizing owned-title libraries internationally; President, CEO & Director Hirsch: "that's part of a big piece of our strategy" including "output deals around the world" and "in the second window" monetization as titles age. (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

  • Brent Penter, Raymond James: asked what engagement came from Universal Pay-2 titles; President, CEO & Director Hirsch: "there's absolutely almost zero viewership or engagement tied to those titles." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

  • David Joyce, Seaport: pressed on subscriber trends; President, CEO & Director Hirsch: "we're not really reporting subscribers" but "total subscribers in the quarter were up even in the face of a rate increase" and highlighted Peacock access to "48 million subscribers" with "14% to 22%" penetration at mature partners. (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

  • Andrew Crum, B. Riley: asked about OTT revenue phasing; President, CEO & Director Hirsch: "we're going to continue to see OTT revenue growth sequentially through the back half of the year" and confirmed Michael timing: "It will premiere on the platform August 10th." (President, CEO & Director Hirsch)

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was neutral to slightly pressing, focused on proof points for owned-content economics, pricing power, distribution/bundling, and visibility into subscribers, including "help us understand what the subscriber trends have been like" (David Joyce, Seaport) and "unpack some of the details" on the price hike (Sean Diffley, Morgan Stanley).

  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and steady in Q&A, repeatedly emphasizing momentum and confidence, including "increase our confidence" (President, CEO & Director Hirsch) and "we remain highly confident" on leverage (CFO MacDonald).

  • Versus Q1, management language shifted toward more explicit upgrades, moving from "We are reaffirming our full year 2026 outlook" (CFO MacDonald, Q1) to "we are raising our 2026 adjusted OIBDA growth guidance" and raising free-cash-flow expectations. (CFO MacDonald)

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Guidance language tightened from Q1 reaffirmation ("We are reaffirming our full year 2026 outlook across all metrics") (CFO MacDonald, Q1) to Q2 increases ("raising our 2026 adjusted OIBDA growth guidance") and a higher free-cash-flow stance within the existing $80 million to $120 million range. (CFO MacDonald)

  • Strategic emphasis expanded from Q1’s Universal Pay-2 exit announcement to Q2’s execution details and financing actions, including "firm commitments to increase our credit facilities by $100 million" to refinance programming notes and "improve annual free cash flow by approximately $4 million." (CFO MacDonald)

  • Analyst focus broadened from Q1’s Pay-2 exit mechanics and subscriber-deemphasis to Q2’s owned-content monetization, Netflix licensing implications, and bundling/packaging dynamics across platforms.

Risks and Concerns

  • "Linear and other revenue was $87 million, reflecting the continued secular pressure on traditional video households we've discussed on prior calls." (CFO MacDonald)

  • "We expect Q3 adjusted OIBDA to be in the mid-30s. This will be our lowest quarter of the year due to higher programming amortization" tied to multiple titles airing in Q3. (CFO MacDonald)

  • "We recorded the associated restructuring charge of $147 million this quarter" tied to exiting Universal Pay-2, with management adding it "sets the company up for meaningfully lower restructuring activity from here." (CFO MacDonald)

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q2 as a momentum quarter driven by engagement highs and early owned-original traction, while updating 2026 financial expectations: higher adjusted OIBDA growth (now mid-single digits), unlevered free cash flow outlook toward the mid- to upper-end of the $80 million to $120 million range, and leverage expected around 2.7x even after a planned $100 million credit-facility increase to refinance higher-cost programming notes. The call also emphasized distribution expansion (Peacock add-on access to 48 million subscribers and a Crunchyroll bundle), continued focus on owned-content economics, and a near-term Q3 profit cadence dip due to amortization before a stronger Q4.

data.title: Amrize forecasts $12.5B-$12.7B 2026 revenue while targeting $3.1B-$3.2B adjusted EBITDA amid oil-driven cost inflation
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Amrize AG (AMRZ) Q2 2026

Management View

  • CEO Jan Jenisch highlighted demand strength tied to “increased mega project demand from data centers and energy to advanced manufacturing plants and infrastructure modernization,” and said the company delivered “strong revenue growth of 8.6%” and “industry-leading organic growth of 6.7%,” while also calling out that “oil price-driven cost inflation drove higher freight, diesel and raw materials costs.” (CEO & Chairman Jan Jenisch)
  • Jenisch emphasized activity across both segments, saying Building Materials had “above-market volume growth, premium cement pricing and leading aggregates pricing growth,” while Building Envelope saw “above-market sales momentum, driven by a strong pipeline of large-scale commercial projects and growth in residential roofing,” with “segment pricing improved sequentially as increases phased in throughout the quarter.” (CEO & Chairman Jenisch)
  • On capital allocation and portfolio actions, Jenisch said Amrize invested “$241 million in CapEx” in the quarter, cited “excellent contributions from PB Materials,” and said “in July, we acquired Rapid Redi-Mix,” which he said brings “significant synergies” in Texas; he also said the company “returned $502 million to shareholders,” and the board declared “a dividend of $0.11 per share.” (CEO & Chairman Jenisch)
  • CFO Baris Oran attributed the quarter’s profitability dynamics to pricing/cost timing and freight, saying, “We saw a significant spike in U.S. freight rates over the past few months as capacity tightened in transport industry,” and added, “As realization of previous price increases reached full run rate and additional price increases take effect, we would expect better net price realization in the second half.” (Chief Financial Officer Baris Oran)

Outlook

  • Management raised 2026 revenue guidance to $12.5 billion to $12.7 billion and revised 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $3.1 billion to $3.2 billion, framing the change around “the timing differences between price realization and oil price-driven cost inflation.” (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • Oran said the company continues to expect cement and aggregates volumes to grow, and updated pricing expectations, stating, “We now expect cement pricing to be flat or up low single digits, and we continue to expect aggregates pricing to be up mid-single digits on a freight-adjusted basis.” (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • For Building Envelope, Oran maintained volume expectations for commercial roofing and raised residential expectations, saying the company “continue[s] to expect low single-digit growth in commercial roofing volumes and now expect[s] high single-digit volume growth in residential roofing for the full year,” while expecting improved price realization in the second half as increases phase in. (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • The analysts-estimates JSON provided in the prompt used a numeric quarter format (not Q1-Q4), so it was treated as invalid per instructions and not used for comparisons.

Financial Results

  • The company reported Q2 revenue growth of 8.6%, net income growth of 14.4%, and adjusted EBITDA growth of 5.8% to $986 million, while Oran said performance was “particularly offset by higher-than-expected freight, diesel and raw material costs” and a “timing difference between price realization and oil price-driven cost inflation.” (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • Building Materials revenue was $2.4 billion and Building Materials adjusted EBITDA was $793 million; Oran cited cement volume up 5% and aggregates volume up 6.5%, along with “strong aggregates pricing growth of 4% on a freight-adjusted basis,” while noting cement pricing was “down 0.2% on a constant currency basis” year-over-year but improved sequentially. (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • Building Envelope revenue was $1 billion, but adjusted EBITDA “was down 5.2%,” with Oran attributing the year-over-year pressure to “timing differences between price realization and raw material costs,” while pointing to sequential pricing improvement and additional pricing rounds extending into July and August. (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • Liquidity and leverage were reiterated as supportive of M&A and returns: Oran said the leverage ratio was 1.7x and the company had about $729 million of cash and cash equivalents with $4 billion of total available liquidity, while maintaining the full-year net interest expense expectation of roughly $340 million. (Chief Financial Officer Oran)

Q&A

  • Anthony Pettinari, Citigroup Inc., Research Division: asked why cement pricing should improve in the second half given “lack of traction in the first half”; CEO Jenisch responded, “We had a slow start to the year,” but pointed to “a 2.1% increase in prices over Q1” and said, “I’m confident we will have a low single-digit cement pricing in the second half of the year.” (CEO & Chairman Jenisch)
  • Adrian Huerta, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Research Division: asked about M&A pipeline; CEO Jenisch said, “Our pipeline is healthy and growing across both Building Materials and Building Envelopes, and I expect more M&A to come,” adding PB Materials is “exceeding our initial expectations.” (CEO & Chairman Jenisch)
  • Trey Grooms, Stephens Inc., Research Division: pressed on Building Envelope volumes and when price/cost turns neutral; CEO Jenisch said the company “gained market share” and expects “a positive trajectory in price and cost to continue into H2.” (CEO & Chairman Jenisch)
  • Bryan Blair, Oppenheimer & Co. Inc., Research Division: asked to “level set” price/cost vs prior framework; CFO Oran said the guidance revision is “entirely related to the duration and magnitude of oil-driven cost inflation and timing of the price realization,” and split the drivers as “roughly 1/3” Building Envelope lag and “2/3” Building Materials factors including cement pricing expectations and freight. (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • Cedar Ekblom, Morgan Stanley, Research Division: challenged the implied margin swing in 2H; CFO Oran explained pricing lags, stating, “Our Building Envelope price increases may experience a 30-day to 90-day lag,” and added fuel surcharges are “at least at a 30-day lag,” while costs are assumed to stay elevated in Q3 with “some moderation in Q4.” (Chief Financial Officer Oran)

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to skeptical on margin mechanics and price/cost timing, led by Morgan Stanley’s Cedar Ekblom saying, “I really just struggle to see how we get a scenario where your margin goes from being down to being flat,” alongside multiple questions pressing on pricing traction and cost assumptions.
  • Management’s tone was slightly positive but defensive on inflation timing, leaning on demand and pricing momentum; CEO Jenisch said, “I think I’m very confident,” while repeatedly tying the gap to “oil-driven cost inflation,” and CFO Oran emphasized expected improvement as price realization catches up.
  • Versus Q1, the dialogue shifted from reaffirming guidance amid volatility to explaining a guidance revision driven by freight and oil-related inflation; management’s confidence in demand remained consistent, while analyst scrutiny increased around incremental margins and the bridge to second-half improvement.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Guidance posture changed from Q1 “reaffirming our 2026 guidance” to Q2 raising revenue guidance to $12.5 billion to $12.7 billion while revising adjusted EBITDA to $3.1 billion to $3.2 billion, with management explicitly citing oil-driven freight/diesel/raw material inflation and timing lags.
  • Building Envelope narrative improved from Q1 being “not where we wanted to be” with a “temporary plant disruption” to Q2 emphasizing record residential roofing revenue performance and sequential pricing improvement, while still acknowledging price/cost lag pressure.
  • Capital return execution advanced from Q1 planning to begin buybacks after results to Q2 reporting $197 million of repurchases within the $1 billion authorization, alongside continued quarterly dividends at $0.11 per share.

Risks and Concerns

  • Management identified the key near-term risk as “oil price-driven cost inflation,” including a “significant spike in U.S. freight rates,” and said mitigation includes “pricing, fuel surcharges and ASPIRE,” with improved price-over-cost expected to “turn positive in Q4.” (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • Building Envelope profitability risk was framed as pricing realization lags on quoted projects; Oran said price increases “affect new projects we are quoting on with a natural timing difference until they take full effect,” and additional increases were scheduled into July and August. (Chief Financial Officer Oran)
  • A year-over-year headwind from lapping insurance proceeds was highlighted, with Oran referencing a net headwind of about $55 million across 2026 from prior-year insurance recoveries. (Chief Financial Officer Oran)

Final Takeaway

Management described a quarter marked by strong mega-project-driven volumes and raised full-year revenue guidance, while revising adjusted EBITDA expectations due to persistent oil-related inflation and freight tightness that outpaced near-term price realization. Executives repeatedly pointed to sequential pricing improvements, additional increases and fuel surcharges, and ASPIRE savings as the path to improving price-over-cost into the second half, with the inflection expected by Q4, while continuing to deploy capital through CapEx, Texas-focused M&A, dividends, and share repurchases.

data.title: Dauch targets $10.6B-$10.8B sales and $1.36B-$1.425B EBITDA as integration run rate savings reach $70M
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Dauch Corporation (DCH) Q2 2026

Management View

  • “The company's second quarter of 2026 sales were approximately $3 billion, adjusted earnings per share was $0.32 and adjusted free cash flow was approximately $148 million.” (Chairman & CEO David Dauch)
  • “We have now been operating for 5 months as a combined company, and we have already realized approximately $70 million of run rate savings to date… We remain on target to deliver more than $100 million in run rate savings by year-end.” (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • “In the second quarter, we won numerous awards with major European, Asian and North American customers… Today, we are actively quoted on more than $2 billion of new and incremental business.” (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • “We will be hosting a Capital Markets Day on November 17 in New York City.” (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • “In the second quarter of 2026, our sales were $2.96 billion.” (Executive VP & CFO Chris May)
  • “For the second quarter of 2026, adjusted EBITDA was $389.6 million and adjusted EBITDA margin was 13.2%.” (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • “We ended the quarter with net debt of approximately $4.1 billion and a net leverage ratio of 2.6x at June 30, 2026.” (Executive VP & CFO May)

Outlook

  • “The company now target sales of $10.6 billion to $10.8 billion, adjusted EBITDA range of approximately $1.36 billion to $1.425 billion, adjusted free cash flow of approximately $260 million to $325 million.” (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Management raised the low end of full-year sales, EBITDA, and adjusted free cash flow ranges versus the prior quarter, stating it “lifted the low end of our guidance range to take into account our performance through the first half of this year.” (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • “North American vehicle production is expected to decline approximately 4% sequentially in the second half, while European production is expected to decline approximately 8%… we are expecting this temporary impact to our production for this program to begin in September.” (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • “We now anticipate GM's full-size pickup truck and SUV production in the range of 1.35 million to 1.4 million units this year.” (Executive VP & CFO May)

Financial Results

  • “Adjusted earnings per share… was $0.32 per share in the second quarter of 2026 compared to adjusted earnings per share of $0.34 for the second quarter of 2025.” (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • “Net interest expense was $82.6 million in the second quarter of 2026… The weighted average interest rate of our outstanding long-term debt was approximately 7.1% at the end of the quarter.” (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • “Net cash provided by operating activities for the second quarter of 2026 was $107.5 million… Capital expenditures… were $91.7 million.” (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • “Our adjusted free cash flow was $148.4 million in the second quarter of 2026 as compared to $48.7 million in the second quarter of 2025.” (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • “During the second quarter, we voluntarily redeemed $125 million of our 6 7/8 notes due in 2028… We now have no major debt maturities until 2029.” (Executive VP & CFO May)

Q&A

  • Gautam Narayan, RBC: Asked whether restructuring cash costs fall in 2027; Executive VP & CFO May said, “We would expect going into '27 that, that number will reduce meaningfully… we do expect those to drop significantly.”
  • Alejandro Nuno (for Joe Spak), UBS: Pressed for synergy buckets and potential upside; Chairman & CEO Dauch said the original split was “30% roughly in the SG&A, 50%… procurement, 20%… operations,” and added, “we're not commenting at this point in time” on raising the $300 million target.
  • Alexander Perry, BofA: Asked why guidance rose with production softness and USMCA implications; Executive VP & CFO May cited “very strong sales” and “good operating performance,” while Chairman & CEO Dauch said, “until we get clarity, it's really hard to forecast what that impact will be,” and pointed to “flexibility… taking over some U.S. facilities… as well as some Mexican facilities.”
  • James Mulholland, Deutsche Bank: Asked what drives reaching the high end of guidance and about the $2 billion quoting mix; Executive VP & CFO May pointed to production, JV income, and synergies ranges, while Chairman & CEO Dauch said, “probably 85% of the business we're quoting today now is ICE and hybrid related.”
  • Nathan Jones, Stifel: Asked about energy/steel inflation and GM pickup content; Executive VP & CFO May said energy was “a relatively minor impact… a few million dollars,” described contractual commodity pass-through cadence of “every 30, 60, 90 days,” and said GM pickup content is “relatively similar.”
  • Thomas Scholl, BNP Paribas: Asked about launch costs and shareholder returns; Executive VP & CFO May said, “I don't see… any period that has overweight launch costs versus the other,” and reiterated deleveraging: “continue to reduce our debt until we're around 2.5x levered or lower.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts were slightly negative to neutral, focusing on cash restructuring, China JV cadence, labor inflation embed, USMCA scenarios, energy costs, and whether synergy upside is possible.
  • Management tone was slightly positive and confident on execution, repeatedly emphasizing integration progress and synergy delivery, including “we're highly confident that we can deliver the $300 million.” (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Versus last quarter, management language shifted from “first time our results include the Dowlais acquisition” to emphasizing acceleration and raising the low-end of guidance, while analyst questioning broadened from definitions/initial integration to restructuring cash, footprint optimization, and USMCA.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Guidance bands tightened and the low end increased in Q2, moving from $10.3B-$10.8B sales, $1.3B-$1.425B EBITDA, and $235M-$325M adjusted free cash flow in Q1 to $10.6B-$10.8B, $1.36B-$1.425B, and $260M-$325M in Q2.
  • Synergy run rate doubled quarter-over-quarter, from “$35 million of run rate savings” after ~3 months in Q1 to “approximately $70 million” after 5 months in Q2. (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Q2 analysts leaned more into operational levers (metal forming margin sustainability, Europe footprint, CapEx phasing, rating agency outlook) versus Q1’s heavier focus on definitional changes, early integration status, and commodity/energy exposure.

Risks and Concerns

  • “Incremental costs related to the elevated energy prices” were cited, with limited operational impact so far. (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Management highlighted uncertainty on trade policy: “We are actively monitoring the USMCA trade discussions.” (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Launch-related downtime risk was explicitly flagged around GM’s next-generation full-size truck transition, with expected volume impacts beginning in September. (Executive VP & CFO May)

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q2 as an integration-and-cash-flow execution quarter, highlighting $2.96B sales, $0.32 adjusted EPS, and $148.4M adjusted free cash flow alongside a $70M synergy run-rate and a higher low-end 2026 outlook. The call repeatedly linked second-half performance to production seasonality, GM’s launch-related downtime timing, continued synergy capture, and balance-sheet actions that removed 2028 maturities and left “no major debt maturities until 2029,” while monitoring energy inflation and unresolved USMCA trade outcomes.

data.title: Manitowoc forecasts $150M-$170M adjusted EBITDA as it raises full-year outlook
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: The Manitowoc Company (MTW) Q2 2026

Management View

  • CEO Aaron Ravenscroft said, "The Manitowoc team delivered great results in the second quarter. Sales increased 10%, and adjusted EBITDA increased over 85% versus last year," adding that "we are increasing our full-year guidance to reflect the strengthening Crane market."
  • Ravenscroft highlighted operational and strategic markers, saying, "we generated strong orders, expanded backlog, increased non-new machine sales, and got our net leverage below our target of 3x," and also noted trade protection: "the U.S. Department of Commerce and International Trade Commission confirmed that Japanese crawler crane manufacturers were dumping... applying import tariffs ranging from 12% to 20%."
  • On product/process and aftermarket expansion, Ravenscroft said the company’s Global Kaizen on a "new 8-axle all-terrain crane" identified "opportunities to expand our aftermarket product offering" including "standardized rigging kits and ancillary products," and added, "We have invested over 100,000 engineering hours in developing this crane."
  • On AI deployment, Ravenscroft said, "we started to meaningfully integrate artificial intelligence into The Manitowoc Way," citing Potain eTech as "an AI agent designed to support tower crane field service techs," and added, "we doubled our users to over 450 this quarter" and that leaders "are required to complete at least 1 AI Kaizen per month."
  • CFO Brian Regan said, "Our second quarter results exceeded expectations, driven by improved operational execution, along with the net impact of tariffs," and added, "orders were strong, with a 1.2 book-to-bill supporting a meaningful increase in our backlog."

Outlook

  • Regan raised the full-year framework, saying, "We are updating our guidance and expect full-year net sales of $2.3 billion to $2.4 billion, adjusted EBITDA of $150 million to $170 million, adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.80 to $1.20, and free cash flow of $50 million to $70 million."
  • Regan described the drivers of the EBITDA guide change: "The bridge reflects the flow-through of the $50 million increased revenue guide at the midpoint, the net impact of tariffs, and variable compensation," and said, "the net impact to adjusted EBITDA of the tariff refunds is expected to be $16 million" while "we expect variable compensation to increase."
  • On risk embedded in the range, Regan said, "The risk associated with the conflict in Iran is considered in our guidance range."
  • Compared with Q1, Regan had said, "we are affirming our previously issued guidance of net sales of $2.25 billion to $2.35 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $125 million to $150 million," whereas in Q2 he said, "we are increasing our full-year guidance."

Financial Results

  • Regan reported Q2 activity levels including "orders of $709 million," "backlog ended at $1.05 billion," and "Q2 net sales were $595 million," and added, "Approximately $750 million of the backlog is expected to ship this year."
  • Regan said profitability and cost metrics improved, including "Adjusted EBITDA... to $49 million" and "EBITDA margin expanded 330 basis points to over 8%," while "SG&A expenses were $90 million" and "on an adjusted basis... $88 million, or 15% of net sales."
  • On tariffs and cash effects, Regan said, "our cash flow benefited from $26 million of cash received related to IEEPA tariff refunds," and added, "the net year-over-year benefit was $9 million during the quarter."
  • Regan reported cash flow and leverage, saying, "Cash flow from operating activities in the quarter was $8 million," "free cash flow was a use of $6 million," "We ended the quarter with $96 million in cash," and "our net leverage ratio was approximately 2.6x."

Q&A

  • Andrew Azzi, Wells Fargo Securities, LLC: "would you be able to help us out in terms of disaggregating... 56% year-over-year growth in orders" by region and how much was "dealer stocking"; CFO Regan responded, "I don't think we share much more color than what we put into the script... but... there's good strength in the U.S." and "demand has been pretty strong everywhere."
  • Andrew Azzi, Wells Fargo Securities, LLC: asked about "cadence of revenue and EBITDA through the second half" and incremental margins; CFO Regan replied, "we have our normal seasonality with Q3 being lighter because of the European holiday" and added, "we do expect about $4 million of incremental tariff benefit in Q3."
  • Submitted question (via Ion Warner): asked for the "IEEPA tariff bridge of $26 million to the $12 million year-over-year benefit"; CFO Regan said, "we received $26 million of refunds and we recognized $12 million in operating income," adding "we have another $4 million coming in Q3" and that other items included "amounts that we're going to refund to customers" and "about $1 million in interest income."
  • Submitted question (via Warner): asked how capital allocation changes with leverage below 3x; CEO Ravenscroft said, "anytime we're below 3x, you know, we're opportunistically looking for share repurchases as well as we're looking for acquisitions."
  • Submitted question (via Warner): asked about July orders; Ravenscroft said, "July was another great month. We're over $200 million" and added, "We'll have to wait and see how August plays out."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts sounded slightly positive and seeking detail, including "Congrats on a great quarter" while pressing for specifics on order drivers and second-half cadence.
  • Management tone was positive in prepared remarks ("All around, it was a great quarter"), and pragmatic in Q&A when narrowing disclosures ("I don't think we share much more color") while still pointing to demand strength.
  • Versus Q1’s more cautious framing around uncertainty ("there is a great deal of uncertainty... with respect to tariffs" and "we find ourselves in a wait-and-see mode"), Q2 language leaned more confident on performance and guide raising ("results exceeded expectations" and "we are increasing our full-year guidance").

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Guidance posture shifted from Q1 "reaffirming our previously issued guidance" to Q2 "updating our guidance" with higher ranges for net sales and adjusted EBITDA.
  • Tariff narrative evolved from Q1 uncertainty and process steps ("we did file our refund" and "wait-and-see mode") to Q2 cash receipt and quantified P&L impact ("received $26 million" and "recognized $12 million in operating income").
  • Market commentary broadened in Q2 toward sustained demand, with Ravenscroft saying, "we see general strength in the region well into 2027" for Asia, while Q1 emphasized resilience and mixed tariff/Middle East uncertainty.
  • Capital allocation emphasis sharpened in Q2 with Ravenscroft explicitly tying leverage to "share repurchases" and "acquisitions," a topic not addressed as directly in Q1.

Risks and Concerns

  • Ravenscroft cautioned that in the Middle East, "shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have stopped" and added, "a prolonged period of regional instability could eventually affect economic activity and customer investment decisions," while saying, "For now, we remain cautiously optimistic."
  • Regan flagged sensitivity in the outlook, stating, "The risk associated with the conflict in Iran is considered in our guidance range," and also noted seasonality, saying "Q3 being lighter because of the European holiday."
  • Ravenscroft cited a Europe product-transition constraint: self-erecting tower cranes are "transitioning to the new EN standards in January" and "our build schedule for these models is sold out for the remainder of the year."

Final Takeaway

Management presented Q2 as a step-change quarter, pairing higher orders and a backlog above $1 billion with materially higher profitability and a raised full-year outlook. The call repeatedly tied results to operational execution, aftermarket momentum (non-new machine sales record on a trailing 12-month basis), and discrete tariff-related benefits, while acknowledging geopolitical risk around Iran and logistics disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz. With net leverage at approximately 2.6x, management also connected improved balance sheet flexibility to potential share repurchases and acquisitions, alongside continued investment in Cranes+50 and the rollout of AI-driven process improvement.

data.title: Ziff Davis expects Q3 revenue down low- to mid-single digits as AI-authored code targets nearly all by end of 2026
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Ziff Davis (ZD) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "During the second quarter, we completed the sale of our Connectivity business to Accenture for $1.2 billion." (CEO, President & Director Vivek Shah) "As a reminder, the acquisition price reflected a 14.5x multiple of the Connectivity businesses trailing 12 months of adjusted EBITDA less CapEx." (CEO, President & Director Shah)
  • "Since our last earnings call, we repurchased approximately 2.8 million shares under a 10b5-1 program." (CEO, President & Director Shah) "Thus far in 2026, we have deployed more than $200 million to buy back 4.5 million shares, reducing the number of shares outstanding by nearly 11% over the course of just 7 months." (CEO, President & Director Shah)
  • "Going forward, a portion of our cash will be allocated to settling our tax obligations related to the transaction, with payments estimated to be approximately $200 million." (CEO, President & Director Shah) "We also plan to repay our $149 million of our convertible debt, which matures in the beginning of November of 2026." (CEO, President & Director Shah)
  • "Our second quarter consolidated revenue across those 4 segments declined 2.7% versus last year consistent with the expectations we set last quarter." (CEO, President & Director Shah) "Adjusted EBITDA declined 3.7% year-over-year, while adjusted EPS grew 13% as we continue to reduce our share count." (CEO, President & Director Shah)
  • "In a single quarter, the share of the code we released that is AI authored has roughly doubled and the majority of new or updated code we released is now written by AI." (CEO, President & Director Shah) "We're currently on track to have nearly all of our code authored by AI before the end of 2026." (CEO, President & Director Shah)
  • "Q2 2026 revenues were $286.7 million." (Chief Financial Officer Bret Richter) "The Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $76.8 million." (Chief Financial Officer Richter) "Q2 2026 adjusted diluted EPS was $1.03." (Chief Financial Officer Richter)

Outlook

  • "We expect our Q3 2026 results from continuing operations to broadly reflect our performance in Q2 2026." (Chief Financial Officer Richter) "Revenues in Q3 are expected to increase sequentially but decline low to mid-single digits year-over-year, while our adjusted EBITDA margin percentage is expected to show modest improvement as compared with this quarter's margin."   • The biggest change was transaction status: Q1 emphasized a "pivot" to monetization with the Connectivity sale pending, while Q2 stated, "we completed the sale of our Connectivity business to Accenture for $1.2 billion." (CEO, President & Director Shah)

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q2 as a post-Connectivity-sale reset, highlighting the $1.2 billion divestiture, stepped-up repurchases, and planned cash uses for approximately $200 million of transaction-related taxes and the $149 million convertible maturity. Leadership described mixed segment demand—ongoing search-driven pressure in Tech & Shopping and softer HCP advertising at MedPage Today—while pointing to off-platform monetization and expanding distribution as key offsets. For the second half, the company guided to Q3 results broadly similar to Q2 with a low- to mid-single-digit year-over-year revenue decline and modest margin improvement, alongside continued emphasis on buybacks, disciplined M&A, and accelerating internal AI-driven product development and efficiency.
